The Four Color Theorem
and Frobenius Algebras

Harry K. Stoltz

October 31, 2026

I want to describe the four-color problem as a question about closed diagrams. Once we have the diagram, we can ask what a graphical proof would have to do.

The Four Color Theorem

Theorem. The regions of every finite plane map admit a proper coloring with at most four colors. Any two adjacent regions receive different colors.

Include the outside region. Two regions that touch only at a point may receive the same color. In this example every pair shares a boundary edge, so all four colors are needed. Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas, The Four Color Theorem.

Graphs

Definition. A finite simple graph consists of a set of vertices \(V\) and a set of edges \(E\), where

\[G=(V,E),\qquad E\subseteq \binom{V}{2}.\]

A graph is planar if it admits an embedding in the plane in which edges meet only at shared endpoints.

An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. Planarity asks for the existence of an embedding. Once an embedding has been chosen, we have a plane graph and can speak of its faces. We use simple graphs for the vertex-coloring statement. The cubic dual may have parallel edges.

The Four Color Theorem

Theorem. Every finite planar graph \(G=(V,E)\) admits a proper 4-vertex-coloring.

\[\exists\,c:V\longrightarrow\{1,2,3,4\}\]

such that

\[\forall\,\{u,v\}\in E,\qquad c(u)\ne c(v).\]
For a map, put one vertex in each region and join vertices of adjacent regions. A proper vertex-coloring of that graph gives a proper map coloring. Repeated adjacencies give the same inequality. Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas.

Tait’s Theorem

Theorem (Tait). The Four Color Theorem is equivalent to the following statement.

Every finite bridgeless cubic planar multigraph admits a proper 3-edge-coloring.

\[x:E(G)\longrightarrow\{1,2,3\}.\]
At each vertex the three incident edges must use all three colors. A bridge cannot carry a nonzero conserved flow. Components can be colored independently. Allowing parallel edges includes the duals of plane triangulations with small boundary cycles. Louis Kauffman, Reformulating the Map Color Theorem.

Planar Duality

Let \(T\) be a plane triangulation. Each triangular face gives a vertex of degree three in its planar dual \(T^*\).

\[e=uv\quad\longmapsto\quad x_{e^*}=c(u)+c(v)\ \in\mathbb F_2^2.\]

The unbounded face has a dual vertex too. Identify the four vertex colors with the Klein four group. Differences around a triangle telescope, and a proper coloring makes all differences nonzero. Conversely, integrate the differences along paths after choosing one starting color. The face equations give path independence on the sphere. Every finite simple planar graph on at least three vertices extends to a plane triangulation on the same vertices after choosing an embedding suitably. The smaller cases are immediate. Kauffman, Reformulating the Map Color Theorem.

Tait Colorings

Identify the edge colors of a Tait coloring with the three nonzero elements of \(\Gamma=\mathbb F_2^2\).

\[\boxed{x_{e_1}+x_{e_2}+x_{e_3}=0,\qquad x_{e_i}\ne 0.}\]
Reveal the three labels in order. Once two distinct nonzero labels are fixed, their sum is the third nonzero element. Conversely, if two of three nonzero labels were equal, their sum would vanish and the third would have to be zero. So the displayed condition is exactly the Tait condition. Each component of the sum is a Boolean parity equation.

\(\mathbf{Rel}\)

Definition. The objects of \(\mathbf{Rel}\) are sets. Its morphisms are relations.

\[\mathbf{Rel}(A,B)=\mathcal P(A\times B).\]
\[(S\circ R)(a,c)\iff \exists\,b\in B\ \bigl(R(a,b)\land S(b,c)\bigr).\]
\[A\otimes B=A\times B,\qquad I=\{\ast\}.\]

The scalars are the two truth values \(\bot,\top\).

Read the composite as first R, then S. Composition asks whether an intermediate witness exists. Tensor juxtaposes independent constraints. The identity is equality, and the dagger is relational converse. A closed diagram can therefore say exactly that a coloring exists.

Frobenius Algebras

A special commutative Frobenius algebra on \(A\) has four generating maps.

Read each diagram from bottom to top.

The four generators are multiplication, unit, comultiplication and counit. The same color denotes one algebra. In the two concrete examples below, comultiplication and counit are the converses of multiplication and unit.

Frobenius Laws

The first row gives a commutative monoid. Turn the pictures upside down to read the commutative comonoid laws in the second row. In the unit column both sides of the unit law are shown.

Frobenius Laws

Frobenius tells us how multiplication and comultiplication pass through one another. Specialness removes a split followed by a merge. Together with the previous slide these are the equations for either spider color separately.

Frobenius Algebras in \(\mathbf{Rel}\)

Take \(B=\mathbb F_2\). Each leg carries one bit.

Equality.

\[Z_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\iff x_1=\cdots=x_n.\]

Parity.

\[X_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\iff x_1\oplus\cdots\oplus x_n=0.\]
These are the two special commutative dagger Frobenius algebras on one bit given by equality and by the group law of F₂, respectively. The equality multiplication accepts equal inputs and returns that value. Red multiplication is XOR. All legs are displayed as predicate arguments using compact bending. With zero legs, both predicates are true in Rel. With one leg, green allows either bit and red forces zero.

Tait Colorings as Diagrams

Write \(x_e=(a_e,b_e)\). On each edge impose the nonzero constraint

\[M:B\otimes B\to I,\qquad M(a,b)\iff(a,b)\ne(0,0).\]

At a cubic vertex, one red spider checks each coordinate.

Follow a single bit from the boundary. A green spider requires the same bit at the nonzero test and at the red spider for its coordinate. Each M reads the two bits belonging to its own edge. The two red spiders impose zero parity across the three incident edges. The six satisfying ordered color triples are precisely the permutations of 01, 10 and 11.

The Four Color Theorem

Form \(D_G:I\to I\) with two parity spiders per vertex and one nonzero test per edge. Green spiders copy each edge bit to both endpoints and its test.

\(\longmapsto\)
\[\llbracket D_G\rrbracket=\top\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G\text{ admits a Tait coloring}.\]

Theorem. For every finite bridgeless cubic planar multigraph \(G\),

\[\boxed{\llbracket D_G\rrbracket=\top.}\]
The picture is the theta graph translated in full. There are two vertices, three edges and six valid assignments, so its scalar is true. In general, composition quantifies over every edge bit. An assignment is accepted exactly when all edges are nonzero and both parities vanish at every vertex. This equivalence holds for any cubic graph. Planarity and bridgelessness enter only in asserting that an assignment always exists. If one glues copies of the previous star, duplicate nonzero tests on an edge impose the same Boolean condition. Kauffman, Reformulating the Map Color Theorem.

The Existing Proof

Reducibility. None of the 633 configurations can occur in a minimal counterexample.

Unavoidability. Every candidate minimal counterexample contains one of them. Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas prove this using 32 discharging rules.

Large dots mark degree five. Small dots mark degree six.

The first picture is the Birkhoff diamond. These are configurations in triangulations, so degree markings refer to the ambient triangulation. In the RSST convention, a large filled circle denotes degree five, and a small dot denotes degree six. The formal structural theorem concerns internally 6-connected triangulations. Reducibility and unavoidability together contradict the existence of a smallest counterexample. Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas, The Four-Colour Theorem. Official configuration data.

The Proposal

For ring colors \(c_1,\ldots,c_6\), port \(i\) carries \(c_i+c_{i+1}\), with indices modulo six. Track which boundary colorings extend and which can be reached by Kempe changes.

Open problem. Derive a uniform reduction

\[D_G\xRightarrow{\ \text{graphical rewrites}\ }\top.\]
On the left is the closed-diagram construction, shown on the theta graph. On the right is the six-port dual of the free completion of the Birkhoff diamond, RSST 0.7322. Going around the ring, record differences in cyclic order. The six differences sum to zero. Choosing the first ring color recovers every other color, so the only ambiguity is a common translation. Phase-free parity alone would allow the all-zero assignment, which is why M occurs on the edges. For example, alternate two colors around this ring. All four interior vertices meet both colors, leaving just two colors for an interior triangle. This ring coloring cannot extend. A reducibility certificate may recolor the exterior by interchanging two colors in a connected Kempe component. Translating that certificate requires the admissible boundary changes and their exterior connectivity. An equality of boundary relations would be a stronger assertion and must be proved for any rule that uses one. The project is to find rules that account for repeated reasoning across configurations and admit a proof of progress on arbitrary admissible graphs. RSST configuration data.

Normalization

Problem. Find a small set of graphical rules that reduce every admissible \(D_G\) to the empty diagram \(\top:=1_I\).

  1. Soundness. Each rewrite preserves the coloring relation.
  2. Progress. Every reachable diagram other than \(\top\) admits a rewrite.
  3. Termination. Every step strictly decreases a well-founded measure.
\[\boxed{D_G\Longrightarrow^{*}\top.}\]

The Four Color Theorem gives \(\llbracket D_G\rrbracket=\top\).
The uniform derivation is the open part.

Here admissible means that G is a finite bridgeless cubic plane multigraph. The rule set and measure should be explicit and effective. The progress proof should use the rules and the planar input structure without invoking the Four Color Theorem. Exhaustive search can already decide existence. Orient the rules with true scalar normal form terminal. Progress must apply after earlier rewrites, not merely on diagrams that still visibly encode cubic graphs. If the calculus uses context-dependent recolorings, the soundness statement must specify exactly what boundary or exterior invariant they preserve. Existence in Rel tells us the target. It does not provide a short rule set or a progress proof. The earlier restricted calculations in this project do not settle that question.

Phase-Free Completeness

Theorem. Two phase-free ZX diagrams of the same type that denote the same binary linear relation are provably equal up to nonzero scalar.

\[\llbracket D_1\rrbracket_{\mathrm{lin}}=\llbracket D_2\rrbracket_{\mathrm{lin}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal R_{\mathrm{proj}}\vdash D_1=D_2.\]

In Z–X normal form, the neighbours of each green spider give a spanning vector for the state.

\[S=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb F_2}\!\left\{\! \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix},\, \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\!\right\}.\]
Normal-form figure from Kissinger and van de Wetering, Picturing Quantum Software, Chapter 4. CC BY-NC 4.0.

Here the semantics is the support relation in LinRel over the two-element field, and the rewrite theory identifies nonzero scalar factors. Bending the inputs of an arbitrary diagram turns it into a state. In Z–X form its green neighbourhoods give a generating set for the support subspace. Different generating sets for the same subspace are connected by graphical row operations. The next calculation keeps the actual scalar factors in the quantum interpretation.

Aleks Kissinger and John van de Wetering, Picturing Quantum Software, Chapter 4, Theorem 4.3.6 and equations (4.11)–(4.15). The illustration is the authors’ original example following equation (4.13), reproduced under CC BY-NC 4.0. Theorem 4.3.6 · The normal-form example · License.

A Normal-Form Derivation

Both green spiders represent \(v=(1,1)\). We keep the quantum scalars as we remove the duplicate.

\(\overset{\textcolor{blue}{(\mathrm{sp})^{-1}}}{=}\) \(\overset{\textcolor{blue}{(\mathrm{sc})^{-1}}}{=}\) \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\)
\(\overset{\textcolor{blue}{(\mathrm{sc})_0}}{=}\) \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) \(\overset{\textcolor{blue}{(\mathrm{sp}),\,Z_0=2}}{=}\) \(\overset{\textcolor{blue}{(\mathrm{sp})}}{=}\)

This is the two-output instance of the duplicate-vector proof in the reading course. Read the top row from left to right, then continue on the second row. Spider splitting leaves the scalar unchanged. Reverse strong complementarity on the 2-by-2 bipartite subgraph contributes the factor one over the square root of two. The nullary instance of strong complementarity contributes the same factor once more. Fuse the disconnected pair of green spiders to a nullary green spider and evaluate it at two. One last spider fusion leaves a single copy of the vector (1,1). All six terms denote the unnormalized state |00⟩ + |11⟩.

Adapted from Harry Stoltz’s Completeness of Phase-free ZX, October 29, duplicate-vector proof, with exact scalar factors restored for two outputs. Aleks Kissinger and John van de Wetering, Picturing Quantum Software, Exercise 4.7, equation (4.12) and Figure 4.1. Reading-course proof · Equation (4.12).

Appendix · Graphs and Maps

Graph
A finite simple graph is a pair \(G=(V,E)\) with \(V\) finite and \(E\subseteq\binom V2\).
Planar graph
A graph admitting an embedding in the plane in which vertices are distinct points and edges are simple arcs meeting only at shared endpoints.
Region
A connected component of the complement of a finite plane graph. The unbounded component is also a region.
Adjacent regions
Two distinct regions incident with a common boundary edge. Meeting only at a vertex does not give adjacency.
Proper map coloring
An assignment of colors to the regions in which adjacent regions have different colors.

Appendix · Colorings

Proper \(k\)-vertex-coloring
A function \(c:V\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) with \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) whenever \(\{u,v\}\in E\).
Multigraph
A graph in which distinct edges may have the same pair of endpoints. The multigraphs here are loopless.
Cubic graph
A graph with \(\deg(v)=3\) at every vertex \(v\). Parallel edges are counted separately.
Proper \(k\)-edge-coloring
A function \(x:E\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) assigning different colors to distinct edges incident with a common vertex.
Tait coloring
A proper 3-edge-coloring of a cubic graph. Each vertex is incident with one edge of each color.

Appendix · Planar Duality

Bridge
An edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components.
Bridgeless graph
A graph that contains no bridge.
Plane triangulation
A connected plane graph in which every face, including the outer face, has a boundary of three edges.
Planar dual
For a connected plane graph \(T\), put one vertex of \(T^*\) in each face. Each edge \(e\) gives one dual edge \(e^*\) crossing \(e\) and joining the vertices of its incident faces.

Appendix · Relational Diagrams

Scalar
A morphism \(I\to I\). In \(\mathbf{Rel}\), the scalar \(\top\) contains \((\ast,\ast)\), and \(\bot\) is empty.
Special commutative Frobenius algebra
A commutative monoid \((A,\mu,\eta)\) and a cocommutative comonoid \((A,\delta,\varepsilon)\) satisfying the Frobenius and specialness equations
\[(\mu\otimes 1)(1\otimes\delta)=\delta\mu=(1\otimes\mu)(\delta\otimes 1),\qquad\mu\delta=1_A.\]
Here juxtaposition of maps means composition, read right to left.
Nonzero constraint
The effect \(M:B\otimes B\to I\) accepts the pairs \(01,10,11\) and rejects \(00\), for \(B=\mathbb F_2\).

Appendix · Reductions

Minimal counterexample
A planar graph without a proper 4-vertex-coloring having as few vertices as possible among all such graphs.
Reducible configuration
A prescribed local triangulation with ambient vertex degrees for which a reduction proves that it cannot occur in a minimal counterexample.
Unavoidable set
A set of configurations such that every triangulation in the class under consideration contains at least one member.
Discharging
A proof method that assigns charges to vertices or faces and transfers charge by local rules while preserving the total.
Kempe change
Choose two colors and a connected component of the subgraph they induce. Interchange the two colors throughout that component.

Appendix · Normal Forms

Well-founded measure
A function from diagrams to an ordered set with no infinite strictly descending chain. Requiring the measure to decrease at every step rules out infinite reductions.
Phase-free ZX
The fragment generated by zero-phase Z- and X-spiders, with identities, swaps, cups and caps. Its relational interpretation on \(n\) inputs and \(m\) outputs is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb F_2^{n+m}\).
Z–X normal form for states
A bipartite diagram with internal green spiders and one red spider for each output. A green spider determines a vector whose \(j\)-th entry is 1 exactly when it is joined to the \(j\)-th red spider. The span of these vectors is the support of the state.
